briefing.text: The hypothesis is a joint claim with two halves: no effect on RNA splicing AND no effect on haematopoiesis. Before any testing, list every file and every column and write down, separately for each half, which columns are a direct readout (for splicing: expression, isoform or percent-spliced-in data; for haematopoiesis: blood counts, blasts, dysplasia) and which are only indirect (which genes are mutated, the mutation pattern, WHO class). The library's reading of the file list is that the study may hold only whole-exome DNA mutation calls plus short clinical tables; verify this yourself. A splicing effect is normally established by RNA-seq of mutant versus wild-type samples, which a mutation table cannot provide. If there is no direct readout, do not write that a splicing change was measured: say that the evidence is indirect, base the label only on what the tables themselves show and not on textbook knowledge of these genes, and assess each half of the claim on its own evidence.
briefing.reason: This decides what counts as evidence for the label. Without it a team can report background knowledge as if it were a result of this data, or judge the whole claim from one half.

briefing.text: A mutant-versus-wild-type comparison with p > 0.05 is not support for a no-effect hypothesis. The cohort is small (about 29 patients; confirm the count), so a non-significant difference is absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect. For every comparison report the group sizes and the effect size with an exact confidence interval, and ask what size of effect the sample could have detected. If the interval is wide and covers both zero and large effects, the comparison is uninformative: do not use it to label the hypothesis as supported; the label must then rest on other evidence or on whether relevant variables exist at all.
briefing.reason: The hypothesis is a null claim, so the most likely error is reading an underpowered non-significant test as confirmation. This changes how every test result is interpreted.

briefing.text: Do not confuse 'splice-site mutations' with 'mutations in splicing machinery genes'. Variant_Classification values such as Splice_Site or Splice_Region mark cis mutations at an intron/exon boundary of any gene; the hypothesis is about mutations in genes that encode spliceosome components. Define the exposure by Hugo_Symbol against a spliceosome gene list fixed in advance (core 3' splice-site recognition factors such as SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2, SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2, PRPF40B, plus a broader list such as the KEGG spliceosome set), never by Variant_Classification or Consequence. Keep splice-site variants in other genes out of the 'splicing machinery mutated' group.
briefing.reason: Filtering on the wrong column defines a different exposure and answers a different question; this fixes how the mutated group is built.

briefing.text: Splicing-factor genes can be missed because the mutation file may use old or alias gene symbols: U2AF35 = U2AF1, U2AF65 = U2AF2, SFRS2 or SC35 = SRSF2, U2AF1RS2 or URP = ZRSR2, SF3B155 or SAP155 = SF3B1. Spreadsheet handling can also turn symbols such as SEPT and MARCH genes into dates. The Entrez_Gene_Id column in data_mutations.txt looks empty, so the symbol is the only key. List all unique Hugo_Symbol values, match them case-insensitively against both current and alias symbols for the spliceosome gene list, scan for date-like or malformed symbols, map aliases to the current symbol before counting mutated patients, and report the gene list actually used.
briefing.reason: A symbol mismatch would silently undercount splicing-gene mutations and could change who is classed as mutated.

briefing.text: Use the right unit and the right denominator. A mutation file lists only mutated genes, so a profiled sample with no call has no row in it; and the patient table appears to have one row fewer than the sample table, so one patient may have two samples. Take the denominator from data_clinical_sample.txt and data_gene_panel_matrix.txt (all whole-exome-profiled samples), compare the set of Tumor_Sample_Barcode values with SAMPLE_ID, count samples per PATIENT_ID, and look for duplicated rows of the same variant in the same sample. Analyse one record per patient (mutated if any of the patient's samples is mutated), treat profiled samples absent from the mutation file as having no detected mutation, and de-duplicate variants before counting.
briefing.reason: Counting mutation rows or only the samples present in the mutation file distorts every frequency and breaks the independence that exact tests assume.

briefing.text: The cohort appears to be case-only: every patient already has a myeloid neoplasm (MDS and related diagnoses, with sample IDs suggesting MDS and therapy-related AML cases pooled), so there is no unaffected comparison group and 'does the mutation affect haematopoiesis' cannot be tested as diseased versus healthy. The haematopoiesis-related variables look like WHO_CLASS, CYTOGENETICS and IPSS_SCORE in data_clinical_patient.txt. WHO class encodes a marrow phenotype (for example ring sideroblasts, excess blasts, monocytosis) but it is a diagnostic category, and associations inside a diseased cohort are conditioned on disease and confounded by subtype mix. Check whether any blood-count, blast or dysplasia column exists. Cross-tabulate splicing-gene mutation status (per gene and pooled) against WHO class, IPSS and karyotype with exact tests and report the table itself. If only class-level phenotype is available, describe any link as an association between mutation and disease subtype within patients, not as a causal effect on haematopoiesis, and say plainly whether the tables hold a direct haematopoiesis measure.
briefing.reason: It tells the team which columns bear on the haematopoiesis half and how far a result from them can be taken, which affects both the tests run and the wording of the conclusion.

briefing.text: The mutation pattern within a gene is the accepted indirect evidence that its mutations are selected and functional: the same codon hit repeatedly by missense or in-frame changes is a hotspot (altered-function) pattern, and scattered frameshift, nonsense or splice-site variants are a loss-of-function pattern. It shows selection, not which molecular process changes. For each splicing-factor gene tabulate Protein_position, HGVSp_Short and Variant_Classification per patient, plus the Hotspot column if present, and note whether hits cluster at one residue, whether any are silent, and whether truncating variants occur. If hits cluster or are consistently truncating, describe this as indirect evidence that the mutations are non-random and functionally selected, and state that the consequence for splicing is inferred, not measured. If hits are scattered single missense variants, treat them as possible passengers.
briefing.reason: This is the main analysis a mutation table can support on whether the mutations are functional, and the team needs to know both how to do it and what it does and does not show.

briefing.text: 'Several patients carry a mutation in some splicing gene' is not by itself proof of selection. A spliceosome gene set holds more than 100 genes and a lot of coding sequence, so with a few hundred somatic mutations across roughly 29 exomes some hits are expected by chance. Fix the gene set before looking at the mutation list; compute the expected number of non-silent hits in the set from the cohort's total mutation count and the set's share of exome coding length (Poisson or binomial); compare with the observed count; count each patient once; and compare non-silent with silent mutations in the set. If the observed count is not clearly above expectation, or the result depends on a list chosen after seeing the data, report recurrence as descriptive only and do not call the pathway significantly mutated.
briefing.reason: Choosing the gene set after the fact, counting mutations instead of patients and ignoring gene length all inflate the signal; this sets the test that guards against that.

briefing.text: 'Wild-type' here means 'no mutation detected'. The germline control appears to be CD3+ T cells, which in myeloid neoplasms can contain clonal myeloid DNA, so somatic callers can drop real mutations; exome capture is also uneven. Some patients may therefore be misclassified as unmutated, which biases mutant-versus-wild-type comparisons toward no difference. The t_ref_count and t_alt_count columns also look empty, so allele fraction, clone size and heterozygosity cannot be computed. Confirm whether the read-count columns are populated and check GERMLINE_CONTROL, SOMATIC_STATUS and Validation_Status. If there are no counts and the control is T cells, make no claims about heterozygosity, clone size or the order of mutations, and state that mutation frequencies are lower bounds.
briefing.reason: Misclassification toward 'unmutated' pushes comparisons toward the null, which matters for a no-effect hypothesis, and it rules out allele-fraction analyses the team might otherwise attempt.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the two teams used different rules for what the task's label definitions mean by a 'relevant variable'. The other team treated the hypothesis as a joint claim with two halves (RNA splicing; haematopoiesis) and judged each half on its own, listing for each half which columns are a direct readout and which are only indirect. Re-read the three label definitions in the task text and write down, separately for each half, which columns in these tables you class as exposure, which as outcome or proxy, and whether the definitions require a directly measured outcome. Was your label rule applied to each half separately? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team recorded that the sample table states which tissue served as each patient's matched normal, and that it is not the same tissue for every patient. Check that column in your data. What does it mean for how 'no mutation detected' should be read, and what, if anything, does it tell you about which blood-cell lineages carry the somatic mutations in the mutation file? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team fixed its splicing-gene list before opening the mutation file, also tested a wider pre-specified pathway list, repeated the enrichment test leaving each gene out in turn, and separated recurrent-codon or truncating variants from single scattered missense variants that could be passengers. Your notes say one of your gene sets was chosen after seeing recurrence. Check which of your gene sets were fixed before looking, and whether your carrier count, exclusivity result and disease-type result stay the same under a pre-fixed list and under a strict definition of a functional variant. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that one of the splicing genes lies on a sex chromosome and that this single gene can by itself create an association between pooled splicing-mutation status and a patient characteristic. Check whether any of your pooled associations, including the disease-type one, is carried by one gene or by the sex make-up of the disease groups, by repeating them per gene and with that gene left out. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the two teams used different rules for what the task's label definitions mean by a 'relevant variable'. The other team wrote its label rule into its plan before running any test, stating which kinds of column would have to exist for each label to apply. Re-read the three label definitions in the task text and write down, separately for each half of the hypothesis (RNA splicing; haematopoiesis), which columns in these tables you class as exposure, which as outcome or proxy, and whether the definitions require a directly measured outcome. Is the hypothesis as worded one joint claim or two claims, and does evidence on one half settle the label for the whole? Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team tested disease type as a three-category table, not as pooled two-by-two contrasts, using an exact permutation test under more than one splicing-gene set, and saw that the result depends on which genes are in the set. Check whether that holds in your data with your pre-fixed gene sets and per gene, and say how much weight a within-cohort disease-type pattern can carry for the haematopoiesis half given the cohort size and how the gene subset was chosen. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found a variant with a splice-site classification that sits in a gene whose own product may be a splicing component, in a patient who also carries a core splicing-gene mutation. You listed splice-site-class variants separately and did not count them as exposure. Check, gene by gene, whether any gene carrying such a variant belongs in a pre-specified splicing-machinery list, and whether your one-gene-per-patient count and your exclusivity test stand if it does. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team compared each sample's mutation-burden value in the sample table with the number of rows that sample has in the mutation file and found a sample where the two disagree. Check whether that holds in your data, and whether a missing row, together with gene lengths taken from memory, could matter for the total and the expected-hit figure in your enrichment test. Does it change your method?

referee.difference: X and Y agree on the rows, the pre-fixed splicing-gene list and every number (29 patients, 260 exome-wide somatic rows, 16/29 carriers, same enrichment). They differ only in the reading of the label rule: X says the recurrence/hotspot (selection) signature of splicing-gene mutations in marrow clones is not an analysis of a relevant variable because no column measures RNA splicing or haematopoiesis, so 'Not verifiable'; Y says that signature is usable evidence against 'no effect on haematopoiesis', which contradicts the joint claim, so 'False'.
referee.test: Pre-registered in prereg.md, code in code/referee_test.py, output in test_output.txt. Calibration of the selection readout using only the mutation table (no external gene lengths): (1) check the table is exome-wide rather than gene-preselected; (2) score a positive-control set fixed beforehand of 14 genes accepted to act on haematopoiesis (TET2, RUNX1, ASXL1, TP53, NRAS, KRAS, CBL, EZH2, DNMT3A, IDH1, IDH2, NPM1, FLT3, JAK2) by number of patients hit, against a null of 100,000 random 8-gene sets drawn from genes present in the file (conservative, since it conditions on being mutated at least once); (3) score the 8-gene splicing set the same way; (4) list every codon hit in two or more patients file-wide.
referee.expected_if_x: The table is gene-preselected, or the positive controls do not separate from the null (readout uncalibrated), or the splicing set falls inside the random-set null or clearly below the positive controls. Then the enrichment is not usable evidence and the data hold nothing that bears on the claim.
referee.expected_if_y: The table is exome-wide; known haematopoietic drivers separate clearly from the null; the splicing set scores at the positive-control level and outside the random-set null (p<0.001); same-codon recurrence is shared only with known drivers. Then the data hold an analysable variable that contradicts 'no effect on haematopoiesis'.
referee.outcome: Y's prediction held on every point. The table is exome-wide: 224 genes in 260 rows, 213 hit in one patient only. Only 11 genes are hit in 2 or more patients: 3 splicing genes (U2AF1 5, ZRSR2 5, SRSF2 3), 7 of the positive controls (TET2 8, NRAS 3, TP53, EZH2, DNMT3A, ASXL1, KRAS 2 each) and BCOR, so the readout recovers known haematopoietic drivers and almost nothing else (mean patients per mutated gene: splicing 2.67, positive controls 2.17, all other genes 1.005). The splicing set hits 16/29 patients, the same as the 14-gene positive-control set (16/29). Random 8-gene sets from the other genes in the file: mean 6.9 patients, maximum 9 in 100,000 draws (p<1e-5); from all genes including the drivers and the splicing genes themselves: p=0.0003. The only codons hit in 3 patients are U2AF1 Q157 and SRSF2 P95; the only others hit in 2 or more are NRAS G12 and G13. The Hotspot column is all zeros and uninformative. The test did not find any direct RNA-splicing readout; that half remains unmeasured, as both teams said.
referee.reason: The disagreement is whether the selection signature is a valid in-data readout. The calibration test shows it is: applied blind to this table it singles out established haematopoietic driver genes and the splicing genes, and nothing else, and the splicing set behaves exactly like the positive controls (same carrier count, more recurrence per gene, canonical-driver-style codon hotspots) and far outside random gene sets. So the mutation table is a relevant variable, and analysing it gives evidence that splicing-machinery mutations are selected in haematopoietic clones of patients with marrow disease, which contradicts 'do not affect haematopoiesis'. Because the hypothesis denies an effect on both outcomes, contradicting one half is enough for False. X's label requires a directly measured outcome, which the task's definitions do not ask for (their 'Not verifiable' example is a variable wholly absent), and X itself stated the label would be False if selection evidence is admissible. Remaining limit: the effect on RNA splicing itself is not measured in these tables, and the cohort is case-only.

questions.question: In cancer genomics, when a gene or pathway shows a positive-selection signature in somatic mutation data alone (mutated far more often than a background model predicts, recurrent hotspot codons, mutual exclusivity among pathway members), how do standard driver-discovery references word what this establishes? Is it treated as evidence that the mutations have a functional effect on the tissue in which the clone grows, or only as evidence of selection that needs separate functional or phenotypic data before any effect on a named biological process can be claimed?
questions.why: Both teams have the same selection statistics and split only on whether that kind of indirect evidence can contradict a 'no effect' claim. The field's convention for this inference would settle how far the evidence reaches.

questions.why: One team recorded the matched-normal tissue and the other did not. Its meaning decides how 'wild-type' should be read and whether the mutation table itself carries information about blood-cell lineages.

findings.question: In cancer genomics, when a gene or pathway shows a positive-selection signature in somatic mutation data alone (mutated far more often than a background model predicts, recurrent hotspot codons, mutual exclusivity among pathway members), how do standard driver-discovery references word what this establishes? Is it treated as evidence that the mutations have a functional effect on the tissue in which the clone grows, or only as evidence of selection that needs separate functional or phenotypic data before any effect on a named biological process can be claimed?
findings.answer: Both, at two different levels. (1) What selection is taken to establish: the standard references define a driver by its effect on the carrying cell, so a selection signature is read as evidence of a functional effect in one specific sense - higher fitness (growth/survival) of the clone in its tissue. Vogelstein 2013 glossary: a driver gene mutation is 'a mutation that directly or indirectly confers a selective growth advantage to the cell in which it occurs', a passenger has 'no direct or indirect effect on the selective growth advantage'. Martincorena 2017 (dN/dS): drivers 'confer a selective advantage on the cell, increasing survival or proliferation'. Tokheim 2016: 'A cancer driver gene is defined as one whose mutations increase net cell growth under the specific microenvironmental conditions that exist in the cell in vivo', and evaluating mutations in clonal expansions is 'the only way to assess the evidence for a gene being a driver gene in vivo in humans'. For blood specifically, Watson 2020 reads selection in sequencing data directly as fitness advantages of haematopoietic clones ('positive selection, not drift, is the major force shaping clonal hematopoiesis'). (2) What it is not taken to establish: the molecular process or phenotype through which the advantage arises. The same literature words statistical hits as candidates / 'significantly mutated genes' (Cheng 2016), warns that methods 'yield many false-positive calls' with no gold standard and that 'only a limited number of genes have been fully vetted' (Tokheim 2016), and says 'statistics of mutations do not identify a change in protein conformation' (Nussinov 2019). Reviews attribute the splicing and differentiation effects of splicing-factor mutations to separate RNA-seq and animal-model work, not to mutation statistics (Saez 2017 abstract). Reach for the teams: by field convention a genuine selection signature is admissible indirect evidence against 'no effect on the growth of haematopoietic cells'; it cannot by itself show an effect on RNA splicing, and in a small cohort the selection call may itself be a false positive. Limit of this answer: no source I read states a formal rule that functional data are required before a named process can be claimed; that half is inferred from the definitions and from how the references word their results.

findings.question: In somatic mutation calling for myeloid neoplasms, what is known about using sorted CD3+ T cells as the matched normal compared with a non-blood tissue such as buccal cells? Can mutations acquired in an early haematopoietic stem or progenitor cell also be present in T cells and so be filtered out, and what does a mutation found in the tumour fraction but absent from the patient's T cells imply about the lineage in which it arose and expanded?
findings.answer: Purified CD3+ T cells are an accepted, well-performing matched normal, but they are blood-derived, so 'somatic' means 'in the tumour fraction and not in the patient's T cells'. Performance: in 16 MDS exomes the marrow-vs-T-cell comparison had the highest calling rate (197 of 245 validated variants, 80.4%) and missed 1 variant; buccal swabs missed 2; skin biopsy missed 51, because of blood contamination. T cells had to be sorted to about 95% purity, and 10 of 26 patients were left out, partly for >5% myeloid contamination of the T-cell fraction (Padron 2018). Against cultured fibroblasts as benchmark, T cells had sensitivity 0.91-1.00 and the lowest false-positive rate, while skin and saliva were inconsistent (Jakobsen 2025, 7 patients). Can early mutations be in T cells and be filtered out: yes. Blood Cancer Journal 2017 states 'the use of T cells is limited by the presence of evolutionary early somatic mutations like DNMT3A mutations that also are present in the malignant clone'. A review excerpt returned by search (the passage was not in the text returned when I opened the page) says DNMT3A clonal-haematopoiesis mutations are detectable in T cells at lower allele fraction than in myeloid cells, while TET2 mutations appear absent from T cells. Residual myeloid cells in the T-cell fraction have the same subtracting effect. So 'wild-type' means 'not detected as tumour-specific relative to T cells', and frequencies are lower bounds. Lineage implication: a mutation in tumour and absent from T cells is acquired and sits in a clone that feeds the myeloid compartment but not, measurably, the sampled T cells. It does not show the mutation arose in a myeloid-committed cell. SF3B1 mutations in MDS-RS trace back to lymphomyeloid stem cells and reach pro-B progenitors, yet show 'little or no' involvement of mature B cells, which the authors call 'compatible with mutated SF3B1 negatively affecting lymphoid development' (Mortera-Blanco 2017); SF3B1-mutant stem cells gave myeloid-restricted engraftment in mice (Mian 2015). Neither abstract reports T cells directly. Because the tumour-vs-T-cell contrast applies to every row of the mutation table, the myeloid-skewed pattern is a property of the design and is not evidence specific to splicing genes. Not confirmed here: the abstract of Shlush 2014 did not load, so the classic report of pre-leukaemic DNMT3A mutations in T cells is not a read source.

findings.question: Which genes make up the conventional 'splicing machinery' or 'spliceosome' gene set used when reporting splicing-factor mutations in myeloid neoplasms, and is LUC7L2 classed as a spliceosome component or splicing factor in standard curated sets (KEGG spliceosome pathway, Gene Ontology mRNA-splicing terms, the usual myeloid splicing-factor lists)?
findings.answer: Conventional myeloid set: a core of four genes - SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2 - plus a commonly reported extension of PRPF8 and LUC7L2. Visconte 2019 names exactly these six as mutated 'components of the pre-messenger RNA splicing machinery'; Hershberger 2020 lists 'SF3B1, U2AF1, SRSF2, LUC7L2, PRPF8, DDX41 and ZRSR2' as the most common of 30+ mutated splicing factors. The original eight-gene set also has SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2 and PRPF40B; I saw those four in search excerpts of two reviews (Saez 2017; Visconte 2012 Table 1), not in the text returned on opening the pages. LUC7L2 by source: (a) KEGG pathway map hsa03040 'Spliceosome': NOT a member - the KEGG gene entry hsa:51631 has no PATHWAY field and 51631 is absent from the hsa03040 gene list. (b) KEGG BRITE spliceosome hierarchy br03041: a member, under 'Other splicing related proteins > Spliceosome associated proteins (SAPs) > Other SAPs' (orthology K13212, RNA-binding protein Luc7-like). (c) Gene Ontology via UniProt Q9Y383: mRNA splice site recognition (GO:0006376), U1 snRNP (GO:0005685), U2-type prespliceosome (GO:0071004); UniProt's function line is only 'May bind to RNA via its Arg/Ser-rich domain'. (d) Myeloid literature: counted as a splicing factor; Daniels 2021 describes LUC7L2 as a paralog of the yeast U1 snRNA-associated splicing factor Luc7p, a 'putative' splicing factor that crosslinks to weak 5' splice sites and the 5' end of U1 snRNA and is 'mutated or deleted in myeloid neoplasms'. So including LUC7L2 follows the myeloid-literature and GO convention; excluding it follows a strict KEGG-hsa03040 definition. Both boundaries are defensible and results should be reported under each. Extra caveat: mapping Entrez IDs from memory (only 51631 was confirmed on a page), the hsa03040 list contains SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, U2AF2, SF3A1, SF1, PRPF40B and PRPF8 but not ZRSR2 (8233) or DDX41 (51428), so a KEGG-pathway-only set would also drop ZRSR2, which every myeloid list includes. Confidence is high for LUC7L2's status and medium for the ID-mapped membership of the other genes.
findings.text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which genes make up the conventional 'splicing machinery' or 'spliceosome' gene set used when reporting splicing-factor mutations in myeloid neoplasms, and is LUC7L2 classed as a spliceosome component or splicing factor in standard curated sets (KEGG spliceosome pathway, Gene Ontology mRNA-splicing terms, the usual myeloid splicing-factor lists)? ANSWER: Conventional myeloid set: a core of four genes - SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2 - plus a commonly reported extension of PRPF8 and LUC7L2. Visconte 2019 names exactly these six as mutated 'components of the pre-messenger RNA splicing machinery'; Hershberger 2020 lists 'SF3B1, U2AF1, SRSF2, LUC7L2, PRPF8, DDX41 and ZRSR2' as the most common of 30+ mutated splicing factors. The original eight-gene set also has SF3A1, SF1, U2AF2 and PRPF40B; I saw those four in search excerpts of two reviews (Saez 2017; Visconte 2012 Table 1), not in the text returned on opening the pages. LUC7L2 by source: (a) KEGG pathway map hsa03040 'Spliceosome': NOT a member - the KEGG gene entry hsa:51631 has no PATHWAY field and 51631 is absent from the hsa03040 gene list. (b) KEGG BRITE spliceosome hierarchy br03041: a member, under 'Other splicing related proteins > Spliceosome associated proteins (SAPs) > Other SAPs' (orthology K13212, RNA-binding protein Luc7-like). (c) Gene Ontology via UniProt Q9Y383: mRNA splice site recognition (GO:0006376), U1 snRNP (GO:0005685), U2-type prespliceosome (GO:0071004); UniProt's function line is only 'May bind to RNA via its Arg/Ser-rich domain'. (d) Myeloid literature: counted as a splicing factor; Daniels 2021 describes LUC7L2 as a paralog of the yeast U1 snRNA-associated splicing factor Luc7p, a 'putative' splicing factor that crosslinks to weak 5' splice sites and the 5' end of U1 snRNA and is 'mutated or deleted in myeloid neoplasms'. So including LUC7L2 follows the myeloid-literature and GO convention; excluding it follows a strict KEGG-hsa03040 definition. Both boundaries are defensible and results should be reported under each. Extra caveat: mapping Entrez IDs from memory (only 51631 was confirmed on a page), the hsa03040 list contains SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, U2AF2, SF3A1, SF1, PRPF40B and PRPF8 but not ZRSR2 (8233) or DDX41 (51428), so a KEGG-pathway-only set would also drop ZRSR2, which every myeloid list includes. Confidence is high for LUC7L2's status and medium for the ID-mapped membership of the other genes. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://rest.kegg.jp/get/hsa:51631, https://rest.kegg.jp/link/hsa/hsa03040, https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9Y383?fields=gene_names,cc_function,go_p,go_c,go_f&format=tsv, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078730/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6966670/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078562/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8394908/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5345729/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3645466/.

the referee's test supported the other answer: The disagreement is whether the selection signature is a valid in-data readout. The calibration test shows it is: applied blind to this table it singles out established haematopoietic driver genes and the splicing genes, and nothing else, and the splicing set behaves exactly like the positive controls (same carrier count, more recurrence per gene, canonical-driver-style codon hotspots) and far outside random gene sets. So the mutation table is a relevant variable, and analysing it gives evidence that splicing-machinery mutations are selected in haematopoietic clones of patients with marrow disease, which contradicts 'do not affect haematopoiesis'. Because the hypothesis denies an effect on both outcomes, contradicting one half is enough for False. X's label requires a directly measured outcome, which the task's definitions do not ask for (their 'Not verifiable' example is a variable wholly absent), and X itself stated the label would be False if selection evidence is admissible. Remaining limit: the effect on RNA splicing itself is not measured in these tables, and the cohort is case-only.
